Lesson five, logs! With dash d, engine x's log seemed to disappear. But it didn't. Docker keeps everything a container prints. Today you'll read it with docker logs, and even watch your own browser visits appear.
First, let's start engine x.
Start engine x in the background, named web, reachable at localhost port eighty eighty, like in lesson four. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker run, dash d, dash dash name web, dash p, eighty eighty colon eighty, engine x. We get a long I D, and engine x is running.
Remember lesson three? Without dash d, engine x's log filled your terminal.
Now, with dash d, nothing is printed. Docker saves the log for you instead.
So how do we read what Docker saved?
With docker logs web. It prints the log lines: the configuration is complete, engine x started its worker processes, and so on.
These are the same lines you saw in lesson three, when the terminal was stuck. With dash d, Docker saved them instead of showing them.
And notice: docker logs prints everything saved so far, then gives you your prompt back.
Now let's see your own visit in the log.
Open localhost port eighty eighty in your browser. The browser sends a request to the web container, and the welcome page loads.
Now read the logs again with docker logs web. At the bottom, there are new lines. The first one is your visit!
Let's read your visit's line, piece by piece.
The first part is who asked. That's you, seen from inside the container's network.
Next, in square brackets, is when it happened, in U T C time.
Then, what was asked: GET slash, which means the home page.
Two hundred is the answer. It means OK, the page was sent.
And the last part tells you which browser asked.
But what is that line with four oh four?
Your browser also asks every website for a small icon to show on the tab. It's called fav icon dot I C O.
Engine x's default site doesn't have one, so it answers four oh four, which means Not Found, and writes an error line. It's harmless, and a good first example of an error in a log.
Is the log too long? Show only the last lines with dash dash tail. For example, docker logs, dash dash tail three, web.
Running docker logs again and again is tiring. So let's follow the log live, with dash f.
docker logs, dash f, web. The terminal is stuck again, like in lesson three. It's waiting for more. Now reload the browser tab.
Look! A new line appears for your visit, live.
Reload again, and another line appears. One line for each visit.
When you're done watching, press Control C, and your prompt is back.
Now a question. Is the container still running?
In lesson three, Control C stopped engine x. What about now? List the running containers. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker P S. And yes, web is still up!
In lesson three, your terminal was attached to the container, so Control C stopped engine x.
Now, your terminal was only watching the log. So after Control C, the container is still up.
So remember: Control C stops the watching, not the container. The page still loads in the browser.
Time to clean up.
Stop and delete web in one command. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker R M, dash f, web. The container is deleted.
Now check that it's gone. List all containers, including stopped ones. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker P S, dash a. Only the header, so nothing is left.
And here's something important. The logs are stored with the container. Once you delete it, its logs are gone too.

Well done! You can read a container's logs. docker logs prints everything the container has printed so far. Dash f follows the log live, and Control C stops watching, not the container. And dash dash tail shows only the last lines. Next, in lesson six, we'll go inside a container!
